Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Troubleshooting
Troubleshooting Common Application Issues
Observe, hypothesize, test, and document using CloudWatch, X-Ray, and CloudTrail.

This lesson collects practical checks and commands you can use immediately when an application is slow, throws access errors, or fails to connect. We'll emphasize a repeatable approach and show a lab you can run to practice.

In this lesson
Identify root causes using metrics, logs, traces, and event history.
CloudWatch
Metrics, dashboards, and alarms to observe health signals.
X‑Ray
Trace requests to find latency and error segments across services.
CloudTrail
Event history for permission and change auditing.
Explore Key Topics
Metrics & Alarms
Quickly see spikes that direct deeper investigation.
Traces
Pinpoint slow segments in distributed requests.
Event History
Confirm who attempted what and why a call failed.

screens.title: A methodical troubleshooting workflow
screens.narratorSegment: A repeatable workflow is the backbone of reliable troubleshooting. Begin by observing system signals: dashboards, alarms, and any user-reported symptoms. Observation should gather timestamps, affected resources, and any recent deploys. Next, form hypotheses that map observed symptoms to likely causes — for example, high C P U could mean an overloaded instance or an infinite loop in code. Prioritize hypotheses that are easiest and safest to test. Then, test with targeted checks: run a Logs Insights query for ERROR entries, inspect X‑Ray traces for slow subsegments, or check CloudTrail for recent AccessDenied events. When a test confirms or rejects a hypothesis, iterate: refine the hypothesis and run another focused test. Always document steps, findings, and remedial actions so future incidents avoid the same guesswork. A common misconception is to change multiple variables at once; that makes root-cause identification impossible. Instead, change one thing at a time and observe its effect. Practically, this approach helps you reduce mean time to resolution, gives reliable audit trails for post-incident review, and lets automated runbooks evolve from documented success patterns. What single, small test will you run first when a system reports high error rates?

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Troubleshooting Workflow
Observe → Hypothesize → Test → Document
A process to reduce guesswork and speed safe remediation.
Step cards
Observe
Collect timestamps, metrics, alarms, and recent deploy history before changing anything.
Hypothesize
Generate likely causes ranked by probability and risk of change.
Test
Run focused checks: queries, traces, small config toggles; change one thing at a time.
Document
Record findings, commands run, and the final remediation so future incidents are faster.
Example scenario
An API becomes slow. Observe increased latency and error counts in CloudWatch. Hypothesize that a downstream database query is slow. Test by viewing X‑Ray service map to locate latency and drill into traces to find a slow query. Confirm with CloudWatch metrics for DynamoDB read latency. Remediate by optimizing the query or adding capacity, then document the change and the before/after metrics.
Common mistake

Changing multiple configuration values at once makes it impossible to know which change solved or caused the issue.

screens.title: Using CloudWatch metrics and dashboards
screens.narratorSegment: CloudWatch is your first, high-bandwidth view into system health. Metrics like CPUUtilization, network input and output, and custom memory metrics provide immediate signals of overload, while error and throttled counters point toward specific limits. Start with the dashboard for a quick health check. If you see sustained 100 percent C P U, that suggests compute saturation; if Lambda Throttles spike, the function is hitting concurrency limits. Alarms are essential: they record when a threshold was breached and often include the state reason so you can correlate with deploy times. A common pitfall is to ignore custom metrics—publish memory or queue depth when the default metrics don't show the problem. Use metric math to correlate counts per second or error rates across services to see whether errors coincide with latency spikes. A practical example: track request count and error rate; if errors rise when request count surges, investigate downstream dependencies for throttling. Finally, always capture timestamps so you can pivot to logs and traces for the same window. What metric would you check first when users report slow responses? Using CloudWatch metrics and dashboards means metrics reveal where to focus: high cpu suggests compute issues, throttles indicate limits, and spikes should map to timestamps for log correlation.. In practical terms, identify resource pressure and error trends that point to root causes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › CloudWatch Metrics
CloudWatch Metrics & Dashboards
Use dashboards and alarms to spot trends and direct deeper investigation.
Key metrics to watch
  • CPUUtilization: sustained highs indicate compute saturation.
  • Lambda Throttles: show concurrency or burst limit issues.
  • Network I/O and error rates: help isolate external call problems.
  • Custom memory or queue depth metrics: useful when defaults aren't enough.
Key Takeaway

Always correlate metric spikes with timestamps you will use for logs and traces.

Example dashboard checks
If error rate rises at the same time request count surges, suspect downstream throttling. If CPU is at 100% while network I/O is low, the instance may be CPU-bound by code or background jobs.
Alarm history CLI
aws cloudwatch describe-alarms --alarm-name-prefix "CohortiaApp" --query 'MetricAlarms[*].[AlarmName,StateValue,StateReason]' --output table

screens.title: CloudWatch Logs & Logs Insights
screens.narratorSegment: Logs are the evidence of what your application executed. CloudWatch Logs stores function and instance output and Logs Insights lets you query and aggregate messages quickly. A practical Logs Insights query filters for ERROR and groups by log stream so you can see which instance or function produced the most errors in a time window. For example, a query that selects @timestamp and @message and filters @message like /ERROR/ will show recent failures; grouping by @logStream yields the noisy resources. When you find an error, read the stack trace and note the timestamp and request ID to match against X‑Ray traces. Avoid searching without a time window—logs are large and queries can be slow; narrow by the suspected incident window. A common misconception is that logs alone answer performance questions; logs show what happened but not where time was spent across services—use X‑Ray for that. Practice forming simple queries to answer focused questions like "which log stream had the most errors in the last hour" and then drill into streams for full context. CloudWatch Logs & Logs Insights means use logs insights to find error hotspots quickly, then use timestamps and request ids to correlate with traces and metrics.. In practical terms, query logs to find error origins and affected resources. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Logs & Insights
CloudWatch Logs Insights
Query and aggregate log messages to find error sources quickly.
Common Logs Insights pattern
filter @message like /ERROR/ | stats count(*) by @logStream | sort by count desc | limit 20
This finds which log streams produced the most ERROR messages in your chosen time window, pointing to the resource to inspect.
Practical advice
  • Always set a time window for Logs Insights queries to reduce cost and latency.
  • Use request IDs from logs to search X‑Ray traces for the same transaction.
  • Look for repeated stack traces and identify the earliest occurrence for regression analysis.
Pro tip

If logs are noisy, add structured JSON logging and annotations so Logs Insights queries can filter on fields instead of text parsing.

screens.title: Using X‑Ray to trace distributed requests
screens.narratorSegment: When CloudWatch shows end-to-end slowness but per-function durations look normal, X‑Ray reveals where time accumulates across services. X‑Ray builds a service map showing nodes like A P I Gateway, Lambda, and DynamoDB and the latency between them. Start with the service map to spot a node with high average latency or high error percentage. Then open traces for a representative slow request and examine segments and subsegments; X‑Ray shows duration and any downstream HTTP or S Q L calls. If a database call takes most of the trace duration, optimize the query or add capacity. Use annotations and metadata you add in code to filter traces for specific users or transaction types. A key misconception is assuming traces are always complete—make sure sampling rates and SDK instrumentation are configured correctly so you capture representative traces. X‑Ray is most powerful when logs and metrics point to a general problem and you need request-level granularity to find the exact slow call. Which trace subsegment would you inspect first when a trace shows a long external HTTP call? Using X‑Ray to trace distributed requests means use x‑ray's service map to find the slow service, then inspect traces to identify the exact segment causing latency.. In practical terms, service maps and trace details reveal where latency accumulates. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › X‑Ray Traces
AWS X‑Ray Service Map & Traces
Locate service-level latency and drill into traces to find slow calls.
Service map insight
The map shows nodes and connections with latency and error percentages. A node with high average latency is your primary candidate for deep inspection.
Use custom annotations to filter traces by user ID or transaction type to ensure you're inspecting relevant traces.
Trace drill-down
  • Open a slow trace and inspect subsegments to see durations of DB calls, external HTTP calls, or internal processing.
  • Look for unexpected retries, long TCP waits, or large SQL results that increase latency.
Key Takeaway

X‑Ray gives request-level visibility that complements metrics and logs, pinpointing the exact call to optimize.

screens.title: Investigating AccessDenied with CloudTrail
screens.narratorSegment: CloudTrail records A P I calls and is essential when your application sees AccessDenied errors. To investigate, filter CloudTrail event history by the event name you expect, such as ListObjectsV2, and by time. The key fields are userIdentity. arn, which shows the IAM role or user that attempted the call, and errorCode or errorMessage, which confirm why the call failed. This evidence lets you change or extend policies precisely. A practical CLI example is using the CloudTrail lookup-events command to find recent AccessDenied events. Once you locate the event, you can confirm the role ARN and the exact A P I name that was denied. Remember that CloudTrail shows who did what and from which IP address, which is helpful when a resource was mistakenly modified or deleted. A common misconception is to immediately change the resource policy without verifying the principal; CloudTrail prevents that by showing the caller. After confirming the principal and the A P I, update the IAM role or policy to grant the minimal, least-privilege permissions required and re-test. Investigating AccessDenied with CloudTrail means cloudtrail gives the who, what, and when of api calls, making permission failures diagnosable and fixable.. In practical terms, use event history to find the api, principal, and error details. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › CloudTrail
CloudTrail Event History
Find the denied API call, principal ARN, and error code to fix IAM issues.
CLI example
aws cloudtrail lookup-events --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=ErrorCode,AttributeValue=AccessDenied --max-results 10 --query 'Events[*].[EventName,Username,EventTime,SourceIPAddress]' --output table
This command surfaces recent events with AccessDenied so you can inspect the principal and time of the failed call.
What to inspect in the event
  • eventName: the API that failed (e.g., ListObjectsV2).
  • userIdentity.arn: the role or user that attempted the call.
  • errorCode / errorMessage: the reason for denial.
Misconception

Don't assume the logged userIdentity is the final decider; it can be an assumed role, so check role trust relationships when needed.

screens.title: Network connectivity issues: Security Groups, NACLs, and VPC Flow Logs
screens.narratorSegment: Connectivity problems often masquerade as application errors. When an app can't reach a database or external A P I, first check Security Groups and NACLs because they are the primary network controls. Security Groups are stateful and typically control instance-level traffic; ensure the EC2 outbound rule and the RDS inbound rule allow the correct port and source. NACLs are stateless and apply at the subnet level, so confirm that both inbound and outbound entries permit the traffic. If security rules look correct, enable VPC Flow Logs to capture accepted and rejected traffic at the network interface level; they show whether traffic is reaching the network stack and whether packets are dropped. Use traceroute or ping from within an EC2 instance to quickly validate routing between the source and destination. A common mistake is to conflate IAM permission problems with network reachability — an AccessDenied is a permissions issue, while a timeout usually indicates networking problems. In practice, check Security Group rules first, then VPC Flow Logs and instance-level connectivity tools to confirm or rule out network rejection. Network connectivity issues: Security Groups, NACLs, and VPC Flow Logs means check security groups and rds/db inbound rules first, then use vpc flow logs and instance traceroutes to confirm packet flow.. In practical terms, how to validate connectivity and find rejected traffic. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Networking
Network Connectivity Troubleshooting
Security Groups, NACLs, and VPC Flow Logs tell you whether traffic is allowed or blocked.
Quick checks
  • Confirm EC2 outbound and RDS inbound Security Group rules allow the required port and source.
  • Verify NACL entries for the subnet allow both inbound and outbound traffic.
  • Use traceroute or ping from an instance to validate network path and DNS resolution.
VPC Flow Logs
Enable flow logs to see accept/reject decisions at the ENI level. Rejected records show whether traffic is blocked before the instance.
Common mistake

Assuming a timeout equals permission failure; timeouts are usually network problems while AccessDenied is a permissions error.

screens.title: Service quotas and resource limits
screens.narratorSegment: Service quotas are account or region limits that, when exceeded, produce throttling or errors. Examples include Lambda concurrency limits, DynamoDB throughput, or A P I request quotas. CloudWatch exposes metrics like Throttles, ProvisionedThroughputExceededExceptions, or Error metrics that indicate you are hitting limits. When you see repeated throttles, identify which resource and whether the limit is account-wide or per-shard. Check the service quotas console or A P I to confirm configured limits. A common remediation is to request a quota increase for legitimate load, or implement client-side exponential backoff and retries to smooth bursts. Also consider architectural changes like using SQS to buffer spikes or using on-demand capacity modes. Remember to monitor corresponding metrics after any change to confirm the problem is resolved. The important point is to differentiate a software bug from an exhausted quota — a high throttle metric points to limits, while exception stack traces in logs point to code problems. Service quotas and resource limits means throttles and error metrics reveal when a quota is reached; remediate with retries, buffering, or quota increases as appropriate.. In practical terms, how throttling and quotas surface in metrics and logs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Recognize throttling signals and choose appropriate remediation strategies.
Signals that indicate limits

screens.title: When the bug is in the code

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Application Code
Instrument your code for diagnosis
Structured logs and trace annotations speed root-cause mapping from logs to traces to events.
Sample Lambda code
import boto3
import os
import json

s3_client = boto3.client('s3')
BUCKET_NAME = os.environ.get('S3_BUCKET_NAME', 'default-troubleshoot-bucket')

def lambda_handler(event, context):
  print(f"Attempting to list objects in bucket: {BUCKET_NAME}")
  try:
    response = s3_client.list_objects_v2(Bucket=BUCKET_NAME, MaxKeys=1)
    print(f"Successfully listed objects: {response.get('Contents', [])}")
    return {
      'statusCode': 200,
      'body': json.dumps('S3 list successful!')
    }
  except Exception as e:
    print(f"ERROR: Failed to list S3 objects: {e}")
    return {
      'statusCode': 500,
      'body': json.dumps(f'S3 list failed: {str(e)}')
    }
Include request IDs and user context in prints and add X‑Ray annotations when possible.
Practical logging fields
  • request_id, user_id, transaction_type, timestamp, and error stack traces.
  • Annotate traces with the same request_id to correlate logs and traces easily.
Common mistake

Relying on unstructured free-text logs makes automated filtering and query much harder—use JSON logs when possible.

Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Lab Walkthrough
Hands-on: Lambda AccessDenied Simulation
Reproduce the AccessDenied, find the event, and fix the role with minimal changes.
Terminal steps (example)
# 1. Create bucket
aws s3 mb s3://cohortia-troubleshoot-demo-YOURNAME --region us-east-1

# 2. Start a Logs Insights query for errors (replace function name)
aws logs start-query --log-group-name /aws/lambda/CohortiaTroubleshootDemoFunction --start-time $(date -v-1h '+%s') --end-time $(date '+%s') --query-string "fields @timestamp, @message | filter @message like /ERROR/ | sort @timestamp desc | limit 20"

# 3. Lookup AccessDenied events
aws cloudtrail lookup-events --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=ErrorCode,AttributeValue=AccessDenied --max-results 10 --query 'Events[*].[EventName,Username,EventTime,SourceIPAddress]' --output table

# 4. Attach read-only S3 policy to the Lambda role
aws iam attach-role-policy --role-name CohortiaTroubleshootLambdaRole --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess
What to observe
  • CloudWatch Logs should show an AccessDenied stack trace when the role lacks S3 permissions.
  • CloudTrail event shows ListObjectsV2 with errorCode AccessDenied and the role ARN under userIdentity.
  • After attaching the policy, invoke the function again and confirm successful listing in the logs.
Lab tip

Record timestamps for the failing and succeeding invokes to make correlation across services simple.

screens.title: Common mistakes and documentation
screens.narratorSegment: A frequent source of repeated incidents is poor documentation and impulsive fixes. The common mistake is changing multiple variables at once or deploying hotfixes without recording the root cause and the steps taken. A better approach is to run one focused test, observe the result, and document the command, console views, timestamps, and the final remediation. This enables post-incident review and conversion into runbooks for fast future response. Another mistake is assuming monitoring coverage is complete—validate that metrics, logs, and traces capture the fields you need before an incident occurs. For example, include request IDs in logs and annotate traces so you can correlate across tools. For assessments, use scenario questions like the ones in this chapter to practice deciding which tool to use: X‑Ray for end-to-end latency, CloudTrail for permission audits, CloudWatch Logs Insights for error hotspots. After each incident, update dashboards, create or adjust alarms, and add documentation so the next responder starts from a stronger position. Common mistakes and documentation means document every test and remediation, and turn successful diagnostics into runbooks and dashboard improvements.. In practical terms, avoid blind fixes and build incident records for continuous improvement. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. fullNarratorScript:
Troubleshooting in the cloud is about information, method, and repeatable checks. In this chapter you'll learn a disciplined workflow: observe system signals, form hypotheses, test them with targeted tools, and document findings. We use CloudWatch to get metrics and alarms, CloudWatch Logs and Logs Insights to read application evidence, X-Ray to trace requests across services, and CloudTrail to prove who called what and when. You'll also learn where networking rules, service quotas, and application code commonly fail, and how to validate each quickly. A practical lab walks through simulating an AccessDenied error from a Lambda function and fixing it by updating the execution role. By the end you'll be able to decide which AWS tool to use for a specific symptom, read a trace to spot a bottleneck, and use event history to resolve permission issues. Keep in mind: a methodical record of steps and outcomes prevents repeating the same guesswork. Ready to practice a repeatable approach that saves hours during incidents?

These objectives outline what you'll be able to do after working through the chapter. First, you'll build a methodical troubleshooting routine so you avoid guesswork under pressure. Second, you'll use CloudWatch metrics, logs, and alarms to detect and diagnose performance and availability problems, and you'll learn how alarms map to concrete remediation steps. Third, you'll interpret X-Ray service maps and traces to find request-level latency or error hotspots across distributed services. Fourth, you'll use CloudTrail event history to investigate permission failures and identify the principal and A P I call involved. Each objective pairs a practical skill with why it matters: organized steps reduce mean time to resolution, metrics give early warning, traces reveal cross-service bottlenecks, and audit logs prove intent and origin for access issues. Together these competencies let you move from observing symptoms to making targeted, safe changes. You will practice these with a hands-on Lambda permission simulation that ties the tools together and reinforces repeatable actions.

Beyond knowing tools, you will practice the checks that give decisive information. You will learn which CloudWatch metrics to trust for initial triage, like CPUUtilization, network input and output, and Throttles for Lambda; how to use alarm history to find when thresholds fired; and how to pivot from a dashboard spike into log search. You will practice writing a simple Logs Insights query to find recent ERROR lines and identify the affected log stream. You will also drill on using X-Ray’s service map to identify the single service that adds most latency to an end-to-end trace, then drill into traces to find the slow subsegment. Finally, you will run a lab that reproduces an AccessDenied error from Lambda and use CloudTrail event history to confirm the calling principal and error code. Practicing these specific checks reduces guesswork, helps you prioritize fixes, and documents evidence for future incidents.

A repeatable workflow is the backbone of reliable troubleshooting. Begin by observing system signals: dashboards, alarms, and any user-reported symptoms. Observation should gather timestamps, affected resources, and any recent deploys. Next, form hypotheses that map observed symptoms to likely causes — for example, high C P U could mean an overloaded instance or an infinite loop in code. Prioritize hypotheses that are easiest and safest to test. Then, test with targeted checks: run a Logs Insights query for ERROR entries, inspect X‑Ray traces for slow subsegments, or check CloudTrail for recent AccessDenied events. When a test confirms or rejects a hypothesis, iterate: refine the hypothesis and run another focused test. Always document steps, findings, and remedial actions so future incidents avoid the same guesswork. A common misconception is to change multiple variables at once; that makes root-cause identification impossible. Instead, change one thing at a time and observe its effect. Practically, this approach helps you reduce mean time to resolution, gives reliable audit trails for post-incident review, and lets automated runbooks evolve from documented success patterns. What single, small test will you run first when a system reports high error rates?

CloudWatch is your first, high-bandwidth view into system health. Metrics like CPUUtilization, network input and output, and custom memory metrics provide immediate signals of overload, while error and throttled counters point toward specific limits. Start with the dashboard for a quick health check. If you see sustained 100 percent C P U, that suggests compute saturation; if Lambda Throttles spike, the function is hitting concurrency limits. Alarms are essential: they record when a threshold was breached and often include the state reason so you can correlate with deploy times. A common pitfall is to ignore custom metrics—publish memory or queue depth when the default metrics don't show the problem. Use metric math to correlate counts per second or error rates across services to see whether errors coincide with latency spikes. A practical example: track request count and error rate; if errors rise when request count surges, investigate downstream dependencies for throttling. Finally, always capture timestamps so you can pivot to logs and traces for the same window. What metric would you check first when users report slow responses? Using CloudWatch metrics and dashboards means metrics reveal where to focus: high cpu suggests compute issues, throttles indicate limits, and spikes should map to timestamps for log correlation.. In practical terms, identify resource pressure and error trends that point to root causes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Logs are the evidence of what your application executed. CloudWatch Logs stores function and instance output and Logs Insights lets you query and aggregate messages quickly. A practical Logs Insights query filters for ERROR and groups by log stream so you can see which instance or function produced the most errors in a time window. For example, a query that selects @timestamp and @message and filters @message like /ERROR/ will show recent failures; grouping by @logStream yields the noisy resources. When you find an error, read the stack trace and note the timestamp and request ID to match against X‑Ray traces. Avoid searching without a time window—logs are large and queries can be slow; narrow by the suspected incident window. A common misconception is that logs alone answer performance questions; logs show what happened but not where time was spent across services—use X‑Ray for that. Practice forming simple queries to answer focused questions like "which log stream had the most errors in the last hour" and then drill into streams for full context. CloudWatch Logs & Logs Insights means use logs insights to find error hotspots quickly, then use timestamps and request ids to correlate with traces and metrics.. In practical terms, query logs to find error origins and affected resources. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

When CloudWatch shows end-to-end slowness but per-function durations look normal, X‑Ray reveals where time accumulates across services. X‑Ray builds a service map showing nodes like A P I Gateway, Lambda, and DynamoDB and the latency between them. Start with the service map to spot a node with high average latency or high error percentage. Then open traces for a representative slow request and examine segments and subsegments; X‑Ray shows duration and any downstream HTTP or S Q L calls. If a database call takes most of the trace duration, optimize the query or add capacity. Use annotations and metadata you add in code to filter traces for specific users or transaction types. A key misconception is assuming traces are always complete—make sure sampling rates and SDK instrumentation are configured correctly so you capture representative traces. X‑Ray is most powerful when logs and metrics point to a general problem and you need request-level granularity to find the exact slow call. Which trace subsegment would you inspect first when a trace shows a long external HTTP call? Using X‑Ray to trace distributed requests means use x‑ray's service map to find the slow service, then inspect traces to identify the exact segment causing latency.. In practical terms, service maps and trace details reveal where latency accumulates. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

CloudTrail records A P I calls and is essential when your application sees AccessDenied errors. To investigate, filter CloudTrail event history by the event name you expect, such as ListObjectsV2, and by time. The key fields are userIdentity. arn, which shows the IAM role or user that attempted the call, and errorCode or errorMessage, which confirm why the call failed. This evidence lets you change or extend policies precisely. A practical CLI example is using the CloudTrail lookup-events command to find recent AccessDenied events. Once you locate the event, you can confirm the role ARN and the exact A P I name that was denied. Remember that CloudTrail shows who did what and from which IP address, which is helpful when a resource was mistakenly modified or deleted. A common misconception is to immediately change the resource policy without verifying the principal; CloudTrail prevents that by showing the caller. After confirming the principal and the A P I, update the IAM role or policy to grant the minimal, least-privilege permissions required and re-test. Investigating AccessDenied with CloudTrail means cloudtrail gives the who, what, and when of api calls, making permission failures diagnosable and fixable.. In practical terms, use event history to find the api, principal, and error details. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Connectivity problems often masquerade as application errors. When an app can't reach a database or external A P I, first check Security Groups and NACLs because they are the primary network controls. Security Groups are stateful and typically control instance-level traffic; ensure the EC2 outbound rule and the RDS inbound rule allow the correct port and source. NACLs are stateless and apply at the subnet level, so confirm that both inbound and outbound entries permit the traffic. If security rules look correct, enable VPC Flow Logs to capture accepted and rejected traffic at the network interface level; they show whether traffic is reaching the network stack and whether packets are dropped. Use traceroute or ping from within an EC2 instance to quickly validate routing between the source and destination. A common mistake is to conflate IAM permission problems with network reachability — an AccessDenied is a permissions issue, while a timeout usually indicates networking problems. In practice, check Security Group rules first, then VPC Flow Logs and instance-level connectivity tools to confirm or rule out network rejection. Service quotas are account or region limits that, when exceeded, produce throttling or errors. Examples include Lambda concurrency limits, DynamoDB throughput, or A P I request quotas. CloudWatch exposes metrics like Throttles, ProvisionedThroughputExceededExceptions, or Error metrics that indicate you are hitting limits. When you see repeated throttles, identify which resource and whether the limit is account-wide or per-shard. Check the service quotas console or A P I to confirm configured limits. A common remediation is to request a quota increase for legitimate load, or implement client-side exponential backoff and retries to smooth bursts. Also consider architectural changes like using SQS to buffer spikes or using on-demand capacity modes. Remember to monitor corresponding metrics after any change to confirm the problem is resolved. The important point is to differentiate a software bug from an exhausted quota — a high throttle metric points to limits, while exception stack traces in logs point to code problems. A frequent source of repeated incidents is poor documentation and impulsive fixes. The common mistake is changing multiple variables at once or deploying hotfixes without recording the root cause and the steps taken. A better approach is to run one focused test, observe the result, and document the command, console views, timestamps, and the final remediation. This enables post-incident review and conversion into runbooks for fast future response. Another mistake is assuming monitoring coverage is complete—validate that metrics, logs, and traces capture the fields you need before an incident occurs. For example, include request IDs in logs and annotate traces so you can correlate across tools. Summing up, follow a methodical workflow: observe system signals, form focused hypotheses, test one variable at a time, and document everything. Use CloudWatch dashboards and alarms to spot metric anomalies and direct your investigation. Use CloudWatch Logs Insights to find error hotspots and timestamps for correlation. Use X‑Ray service maps and traces to locate latency and error segments across distributed services. Use CloudTrail event history to identify the precise A P I call, principal, and error code when permissions fail. For networking issues, validate Security Groups and NACLs and use VPC Flow Logs to capture rejected traffic. Finally, recognize service quota signals like throttles and plan buffering, retries, or quota changes accordingly.
